implementation_notes: The standard library has no resequencer: heapq (or queue.PriorityQueue) supplies the ordered window and the gap policy comes from asyncio.wait_for/asyncio.timeout in async code or threading.Condition.wait(timeout) in threaded code, but the expected-sequence cursor, the capacity bound and the duplicates policy are application code. sortedcontainers.SortedList is the natural upgrade when the window needs keyed removal instead of heap scans. When the disorder comes from parallel workers, an asyncio.TaskGroup or an executor with results collected through one priority queue is often cheaper than buffering elsewhere.
code_sketch:
window: list[tuple[int, Msg]] = []      # min-heap by sequence number
expected = 1
def accept(seq: int, msg: Msg, gap_expired: Callable[[], bool]) -> list[Msg]:
    heapq.heappush(window, (seq, msg))
    ready: list[Msg] = []
    while window and (window[0][0] == expected or gap_expired()):
        seq_, m = heapq.heappop(window)   # in-sequence run
        expected = seq_ + 1
        ready.append(m)
    return ready                          # caller forwards via one ordered queue
pitfalls: heapq compares tuples element-wise, so two messages with the same sequence number fall through to comparing the messages themselves; a counter tie-breaker or a dict keyed by sequence avoids TypeError.
asyncio.wait_for cancels the awaited task on timeout, so it belongs around the delay, not around the delivery: a late message must not cancel work that was already accepted.
threading.Condition.wait(timeout) wakes spuriously and must be re-checked in a while loop, with the gap deadline recomputed from a monotonic clock each iteration.
GIL-protected dicts and heaps are not a synchronisation design: multi-threaded resequencers still need the lock to make cursor and window updates atomic together.
